title: Cabinet clears Rs 2,814-cr critical mineral processing scheme and Rs 17,500-cr energy storage scheme
where: Economy, page 13 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box on energy storage
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Industrial policy; Investment models (viability gap funding) · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources (critical minerals) · GS2 › Government policies and interventions
summary: The Cabinet approved a Rs 2,814-crore capex scheme (30% capital subsidy) for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, and a Rs 17,500-crore viability gap funding scheme for 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage.
evolution: To ease the energy transition, ramp up storage and strengthen transmission.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal for the next 10–11 years.
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: Processing is the chokepoint: India has little processing capacity and is almost 100% import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon, while China dominates processing and uses it as leverage in trade tensions.
GS3 · Mineral security / GS2 · Strategic vulnerability
Mining alone is not enough: control of processing decides who holds leverage in the critical mineral value chain.

Targeted capex support: a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium plants (30 kt each) and two nickel plants (50 kt each), capped at Rs 500 crore and Rs 900 crore per beneficiary, serving EVs, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for lithium and nickel plants aim to build the missing middle of India's battery value chain.

Mineral-specific parks: Gujarat (heavy rare earths) and Andhra Pradesh (a rare earth corridor), Odisha for nickel (reserves, and an eastern location for imports from Indonesia), Maharashtra for lithium, each as a complete ecosystem; a stockpiling policy is also being drafted.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Mineral security
Siting each processing park where reserves, skills or import routes exist applies the logic of resource-based industrial location.

Storage closes the renewable gap: Rs 17,500 crore (2026-27 to 2030-31) for 92 GWh (30 GWh battery storage, 60 GWh pumped hydro, 2 GWh emerging technologies), equal to 170% of existing grid-scale capacity, because renewable power is abundant in some hours and short in others.
GS3 · Energy infrastructure
Energy storage turns intermittent solar and wind into dependable power, the missing link of India's transition.

Market design plus Make in India: storage capacity will be allocated through tariff-based competitive bidding, discoms are eligible for VGF, and battery projects must meet a 40% domestic content requirement, linking storage demand to domestic manufacturing.
GS3 · Investment models (VGF) / Make in India
Viability gap funding with competitive bidding and domestic content rules uses public money to crowd in private investment and local manufacturing.
keywords: Viability Gap Funding (VGF)
A capital grant that makes a socially needed but commercially weak project viable
GS3 · Investment models
VGF for storage bridges the gap between high upfront costs and affordable tariffs.
Pumped hydro storage
Pumping water uphill with surplus power and releasing it through turbines at peak demand
GS3 · Energy
Pumped hydro, two-thirds of the new storage target, is an old technology with a new role in the energy transition.
Domestic Content Requirement (DCR)
A rule that a share of a project's components be made in India
GS3 · Industrial policy
A 40% DCR ties battery storage demand to India's own manufacturing base.
Strategic stockpile
A reserve of critical minerals to guard against supply disruptions
GS3 · Mineral security
A critical mineral stockpile does for batteries what strategic petroleum reserves do for oil.
Intermittency
Variability of solar and wind output across hours and seasons
GS3 · Renewable energy
Storage is the answer to intermittency, which grows with every gigawatt of solar added.
data: 54 GWh now; 411 GWh target by 2031-32
India's grid-scale energy storage capacity and its target
Government of India (Union Cabinet), via IE
GS3 · Energy storage
India has about 54 GWh of grid-scale storage against a target of 411 GWh by 2031-32: a near eightfold scale-up is needed.
examples: Odisha chosen for nickel processing
Domestic reserves plus an eastern location to process nickel imported from Indonesia
GS1 · Industrial location · GS3 · Mineral security
Odisha's nickel park shows industrial location balancing local resources with access to imported ore.
Storage VGF scheme (92 GWh)
30 GWh batteries, 60 GWh pumped hydro, 2 GWh new technologies
GS3 · Energy transition · Investment models
The Rs 17,500-crore storage VGF is a ready example of public funds crowding in about Rs 97,600 crore of investment.
pyqs: Key challenges to India's energy security; measures with growth and sustainability.
Will India meet 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030? Role of shifting subsidies.
Status and targets for renewable energy; National Programme on LEDs.
Can regional resource-based manufacturing promote employment in India?
Multi-dimensional implications of the uneven distribution of mineral oil in the world.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewable targets and solar costs (2015, 2016) to whether India can meet 50% renewables by 2030 (2022) and, in 2026, energy security with growth and sustainability. Mineral questions so far asked about the distribution of resources (2021) and the environmental hazards of mining (2025).
trend.watch: Energy security was asked in 2026 (GS3) and 2025 (GS2), so it is a must-study area. The next step is likely the transition's own dependencies: storage, grids and critical minerals.
focus: Storage and grid integration of renewables
Critical mineral value chains and dependence on China
Investment models for clean energy (VGF, PLI, competitive bidding)

potential: "Energy storage is the missing link in India's renewable energy transition." Discuss. (10 marks)
Why is processing, rather than mining, the weakest link in India's critical mineral value chain? Examine the steps taken to address it. (15 marks)
What is viability gap funding? Explain its role in promoting grid-scale energy storage in India. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Energy storage is the missing link in India's renewable energy transition." Discuss.
parts: Why storage is the missing link

answer.t: In November 2026 the Cabinet approved Rs 17,500 crore of viability gap funding for 92 GWh of storage, as India has only about 54 GWh against a target of 411 GWh by 2031-32.

answer.h: Why storage is the missing link

pts.t: Solar and wind are abundant in some hours and short in others, so supply must be shifted in time.
pts.ex: Solar peaks at noon, demand peaks in the evening.

pts.t: Storage balances sudden swings in renewable output.
pts.ex: Sri Lanka's 2026 blackout from rooftop solar disconnecting (IE, 4 Nov 2026).

pts.t: Surplus renewable power can be stored instead of wasted.
Stored power can meet evening peaks now met by thermal plants.
Storage makes the 500 GW non-fossil target usable round the clock.
pts.ex: PM's 500 GW goal (Nov 2026).

pts.t: Battery demand can anchor domestic manufacturing.
pts.ex: 40% domestic content rule for battery projects.

pts.t: Storage projects are capital-heavy, so tariffs are high without support.
Batteries need lithium and nickel that India imports almost entirely.
Financially stressed utilities struggle to pay for storage.
Sites, land and environmental clearances take time.
Few markets yet reward storage for balancing services.
Competitive bidding with capital support.
pts.ex: 92 GWh VGF scheme.

pts.t: Processing capacity and stockpiles.
pts.ex: Rs 2,814-crore processing scheme; NCMM stockpile.

pts.t: Batteries for short duration, pumped hydro for longer.
Pay for ancillary and balancing services.
Recover battery minerals to reduce import needs.

answer.t: Adding solar and wind builds India's clean power; storage makes it dependable, so the transition will move only as fast as storage does.

title: Bengal's new industry policy thinks outside the box: Pooling land to taking back unused land
syllabus: GS3 › Land reforms; Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Investment models · GS2 › Government policies and interventions (state); e-governance and transparency · GS4 › Fairness and transparency in land allotment
summary: West Bengal's Investment Promotion Policy, 2026 proposes direct purchase of land, land pooling and taking back unused industrial land, with production required within three years of allotment.
ideas: Land is the binding constraint: large contiguous plots are not available as land is fragmented into small holdings, so pooling is proposed to create large areas for major industries.
GS3 · Land reforms / industrial policy
Fragmented holdings make land the main bottleneck to industry, which land pooling seeks to solve.
Consent over coercion: the state wants to buy land directly rather than acquire it ('We do not want another Singur or Nandigram'), learning from the movements that ended the Left Front's rule.
GS3 · Land acquisition / GS2 · Governance
Bengal's shift from acquisition to purchase and pooling reflects the political lesson of Singur and Nandigram: consent sustains industry.
Use it or lose it: production must begin within three years of allotment, land cannot be used for other purposes, unused industrial land will be recovered, and brownfield redevelopment gets priority.
GS3 · Efficient use of land
A three-year 'use it or lose it' clause stops land hoarding by investors.

Transparency by design: a GIS-enabled inventory of industrial land (ownership, plot size, use, connectivity, utilities, encumbrances), published criteria, online applications, time-stamped scrutiny and disclosure of decisions.
GS2 · E-governance and transparency
A GIS land inventory with online, time-stamped allotment cuts discretion and the scope for corruption.

Safeguards and inclusion: land support does not exempt units from land-use, environment, rehabilitation, tenancy, forest or coastal laws; the policy favours labour-intensive industries and MSMEs employing more women and transgender people. Pooling terms are yet to be detailed.
GS3 · Inclusive industrialisation
Land support must not bypass rehabilitation and environmental law, or today's investment becomes tomorrow's Singur.
keywords: Land pooling
Landowners pool plots for development and get back a share of developed land or benefits
GS3 · Land policy
Land pooling makes landowners partners in development rather than displaced sellers.
Brownfield redevelopment
Reusing previously developed or idle industrial land
GS3 · Industry / land use
Brownfield redevelopment brings industry without taking new farmland.
Land bank
A government-maintained inventory of land ready for allotment
GS3 · Investment climate
A GIS land bank cuts the time investors spend searching for land.
Use-it-or-lose-it clause
A condition that allotted land must be used within a set time or be taken back
GS3 · Efficient land use
Use-it-or-lose-it clauses turn allotted land into factories, not speculation.
examples: 'No more Singur or Nandigram'
Bengal shifts from acquisition to direct purchase and pooling
GS4
GS3 · Land acquisition · GS4 · Consent and fairness
Singur and Nandigram remain India's lesson that industry built without consent cannot last.
GIS-enabled industrial land inventory
Online, time-stamped allotment with disclosed decisions
GS4
GS2 · E-governance · GS4 · Transparency
A public, GIS-based land inventory is an example of technology reducing discretion in allotment.
pyqs: Key issues addressed by the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
Why industrial growth lagged GDP after reforms; can recent industrial policy changes help?
Manufacturing's share in GDP, especially MSMEs; present policies.
Drafting a fair compensation-cum-rehabilitation policy for persons displaced by projects.

trend.t: Land questions have tested the 2013 land acquisition law (2014) and, repeatedly, land reforms in agriculture (2013, 2016, 2021, 2023, 2024). Industrial policy questions asked why manufacturing lags (2017, 2023). GS4 asked for a fair rehabilitation policy (2016).
trend.watch: Land reforms recur most years in GS3, so land is a must-study area; questions on land for industry, consent and rehabilitation can draw on new state policies such as pooling.
focus: Land acquisition vs land pooling vs direct purchase
Land as a constraint on manufacturing

potential: "Land pooling is a more democratic alternative to land acquisition." Critically examine. (10 marks)

title: Attracting foreign capital needs more than tax cuts
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy and issues relating to mobilisation of resources; Investment models; Effects of liberalisation on the economy · GS4 › Fairness and impartiality in public policy
summary: With foreign portfolio investors pulling money out of Indian equities, the editorial argues that capital gains tax cuts alone will not bring them back; India needs a competitive regulatory and tax framework, without discriminating against domestic investors or curbing outflows.
ideas: Global pull factors, not just tax: capital is chasing companies across the AI value chain, where India has no significant presence, while rising US bond yields raise the risk-free return.
GS3 · Investment / Globalisation
FPI outflows reflect global shifts, AI-led allocation and higher US yields, more than India's tax rates.
Valuations and earnings matter: corporate earnings expectations and high valuations also drove investors out, so tax concessions cannot be the main driver of market performance.
GS3 · Capital markets
Tax cuts cannot fix markets where earnings growth and valuations fail to justify the price.
Compete as a jurisdiction: to attract capital and become a global financial centre, India needs a regulatory and tax framework competitive with friendlier jurisdictions.
GS3 · Mobilisation of resources
Predictable regulation and a competitive tax regime, not one-off sops, make a country a global financial centre.
Some steps taken: in June the government exempted interest income and capital gains and eased norms to draw foreign investors into government bonds.
GS3 · Government borrowing / Investment
Opening government bonds to foreign investors widens the pool of finance for the state.
Fairness and openness: favouring dollar investors over rupee investors would be discriminatory, and curbing Indians' outward remittances to hold capital in would be a step backwards.
GS3 · Liberalisation / GS4 · Fairness
Policy for foreign capital must stay fair to domestic investors and keep India open in both directions.
keywords: Risk-free rate
Return on the safest asset, usually US government bonds
GS3 · Capital flows
When the US risk-free rate rises, emerging markets must offer more to keep foreign capital.
Hot money
Short-term portfolio capital that moves quickly across borders
GS3 · External sector
Dependence on hot money makes markets and the rupee vulnerable to sudden outflows.
Jurisdictional competitiveness
How a country's rules and taxes compare with rival destinations for capital
GS3 · Investment
Capital flows to jurisdictions that are predictable, not only cheap.
Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)
RBI route that lets residents send money abroad up to a limit
GS3 · Capital account
Curbs on LRS outflows would reverse India's gradual capital account liberalisation.
Tax neutrality
Treating similar income alike regardless of who earns it
GS3 · Taxation / GS4 · Fairness
Tax neutrality between dollar and rupee investors keeps policy fair and credible.
examples: AI-led capital allocation
Investors funding Nvidia, Google, Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC across the AI chain
GS3 · Investment · Science and technology
Global capital chasing the AI value chain shows why technology capability now decides investment flows.
Opening government bonds to foreign investors
June tax exemptions and eased norms
GS3 · Mobilisation of resources
Easing foreign access to government bonds is an example of tapping global savings for public finance.
'If you pitch for dollar investors, what about rupee investors?'
Finance Minister's caution on tax concessions
GS4
GS3 · Taxation · GS4 · Fairness in policy
The FM's question captures the ethical test of fairness in policy: favouring one group must not wrong another.
pyqs: Need for FDI, the gap between MoUs and actual FDI, and remedies.
Challenges as the world moves from free trade and multilateralism to protectionism.
Investment as capital formation; designing concession agreements.
Infrastructure investment for rapid and inclusive growth.

trend.t: Investment questions began with FDI in specific sectors (retail and defence, 2013–2014) and the FDI implementation gap (2016), then moved to investment as capital formation and PPP design (2020–2022). In 2025 the frame widened to a deglobalising world of protectionism.
trend.watch: UPSC asks about foreign capital through FDI and the global economic climate, not market details. Link FPI flows to global shifts, competitiveness and reforms.
focus: FDI vs FPI: role and risks
What makes India attractive: regulation, tax, stability
Global headwinds: deglobalisation, rising US yields, AI race

potential: "Tax incentives alone cannot make India a preferred destination for global capital." Discuss with reference to recent foreign portfolio outflows. (15 marks)
Distinguish between FDI and FPI. Why is excessive reliance on portfolio flows a risk for an emerging economy? (10 marks)
What reforms are needed for India to become a global financial centre? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Tax incentives alone cannot make India a preferred destination for global capital." Discuss with reference to recent foreign portfolio outflows.
parts: Role and limits of tax incentives

answer.t: Foreign portfolio investors have pulled large sums out of Indian equities since 2024-25, prompting calls to cut capital gains tax; the Finance Minister has cautioned that tax is not the main driver of markets.

pts.t: Global capital is flowing to companies across the AI chain, where India has little presence.
pts.ex: Nvidia, Google, Samsung, SK Hynix, TSMC.

pts.t: Higher returns on US bonds raise the risk-free rate and pull money back to developed markets.
Indian stocks priced high relative to earnings growth lose appeal.
Wars, tariffs and protectionism make investors cautious about emerging markets.
pts.ex: West Asia war; US tariffs.

pts.t: A weakening rupee cuts dollar returns for foreign investors.
Past episodes such as retrospective taxation (2012, repealed in 2021) still shape perceptions of risk.

answer.h: Role and limits of tax incentives

pts.t: Exemptions can tilt decisions in targeted areas.
pts.ex: June exemptions to draw foreign investors into government bonds.

pts.t: No tax cut compensates for weak earnings or a missing AI ecosystem.
Concessions reduce revenue without assured inflows.
Favouring dollar over rupee investors breaks tax neutrality.
pts.ex: FM: 'what about rupee investors?'

pts.t: Competing on tax alone invites a contest that small, low-tax jurisdictions win.
Simple, stable rules comparable to leading financial centres.
pts.ex: GIFT City IFSC as a test bed.

pts.t: Semiconductors, data centres and AI firms give investors India-linked AI exposure.
pts.ex: India Semiconductor Mission.

pts.t: Inclusion and easier access widen stable, long-term foreign participation.
Encourage FDI and long-term funds over hot money.
Avoid retrospective or sudden changes in tax and rules.
Do not curb outward remittances under the LRS; openness signals confidence.

answer.t: Capital follows growth, predictability and technology; India wins it back by being a competitive, fair and open jurisdiction, not by tax cuts alone.

title: Companies may be selective, but pvt capex picking up: FM
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: growth, development and employment; Industrial policy (MSMEs, PLI); Investment · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Governance · GS4 › Trust and public service values in governance
summary: The Finance Minister said private investment is picking up selectively after the GST 2.0 reforms, MSMEs are being helped to grow through a new definition, and the PLI scheme's weaker sectors will be examined, with trust in citizens as the government's charter.
evolution: Jan Vishwas and trust-based reforms: the challenge is wages, not jobs.
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
FM: MSMEs must grow from micro to large; policy built on trusting people.
ideas: Demand-led investment revival: the FM said GST 2.0 reforms made consumption and demand visible, so industry is investing again, though selectively in chosen sectors.
GS3 · Investment / Growth
Private capex follows visible demand: consumption recovery is the trigger for a sustained investment cycle.
Micro should not remain dwarfs: the revised MSME definition lets micro firms grow into small, small into medium and medium into large while keeping benefits.
GS3 · MSMEs / Industrial policy
Removing the penalty on growth helps India fill its 'missing middle' of mid-sized firms.
Beyond a few big firms: the FM rejected the view that a few large groups dominate the economy, citing flourishing MSMEs and fast-growing startups and unicorns.
GS3 · Industry structure
A broad base of MSMEs and startups, not a few conglomerates, makes growth inclusive and resilient.
Incentives tied to performance: PLI pays only for additional production; it has worked, but sectors that underperformed will be examined.
GS3 · Industrial policy (PLI)
Linking incentives to output, and reviewing failures, keeps industrial policy accountable.
Trust as the charter of governance: GST, income tax and other policies are framed on trusting businesses, farmers, taxpayers and citizens, with active, continuous dialogue with industry.
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Trust
A trust-based state treats citizens as partners, cutting compliance burden and building cooperation.
keywords: Missing middle
Too few mid-sized firms between many tiny ones and a few large ones
GS3 · MSMEs
India's missing middle keeps productivity low; helping MSMEs scale up is the cure.
Graduation penalty
Loss of benefits that deters a firm from growing beyond a size limit
GS3 · Industrial policy
A revised MSME definition removes the graduation penalty that kept firms small.
Demand visibility
Clarity about future demand that gives firms confidence to invest
GS3 · Investment
Visible consumption demand, not tax breaks alone, revives private capex.
Trust-based governance
Policy that presumes citizens are honest and reduces control
GS2 · Governance / GS4
Trust-based governance shifts the state from suspicion to facilitation.
Performance-linked incentives
Support paid only on measurable output
GS3 · PLI
Performance-linked incentives make public money pay only for results.
data: Share of India's exports from the MSME sector
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, via IE
GS3 · MSMEs / Exports
MSMEs account for about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister), so their growth is export growth.
examples: Revised MSME definition
Lets enterprises grow while keeping benefits
GS3 · Industrial policy · MSMEs
The revised MSME definition shows how policy can reward growth instead of penalising it.
PLI's performance condition
Incentive only for additional production
GS3 · Industrial policy · GS2 · Accountability
PLI paying only for extra output is an example of outcome-based public spending.
'We trust the taxpayer'
FM on trust as the basis of GST and income tax policy
GS4
GS2 · Governance · GS4 · Trust and public service values
The FM's stated charter of trusting taxpayers is an example of trust-based, citizen-centric governance.
pyqs: Manufacturing share and MSMEs for faster growth; present policies.
Rationale, achievements and improvement of the PLI scheme.
Industrial growth lagging GDP and recent industrial policy changes.
Labour-led growth and a growth pattern that creates more jobs.

trend.t: Industrial questions moved from why manufacturing lagged (2017) to MSMEs and manufacturing share in GDP (2023), then to evaluating specific tools such as PLI (2025) amid protectionism. The direction is clear: from describing the problem to judging policy instruments.
trend.watch: UPSC now asks you to evaluate schemes: rationale, achievements, improvements. Know PLI, the MSME definition, credit schemes and their limits.
focus: MSMEs: scaling up and the missing middle

potential: Why do most Indian MSMEs remain small? Discuss the 'missing middle' problem and suggest measures to help them scale up. (15 marks)
"Private investment follows demand, not incentives." Examine in the context of India's recent capex cycle. (10 marks)
What is trust-based governance? How does it change the relationship between the state and citizens? (10 marks)

practice.q: Why do most Indian MSMEs remain small? Discuss the 'missing middle' problem and suggest measures to help them scale up.
parts: Measures to help them scale up

answer.t: MSMEs produce about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister, Nov 2026), yet most stay micro; the government says it wants micro firms to grow into small, medium and large ones.

pts.t: Firms lose subsidies, reservations and tax benefits once they cross size limits, so they stay small.
pts.ex: The revised definition aims to remove this.

pts.t: Lack of collateral and formal records limits access to bank loans.
Large buyers and governments pay late, choking working capital.
Many inspections, filings and licences cost more for small firms.
pts.ex: Jan Vishwas decriminalisation is a response.

pts.t: Old machines and untrained workers keep productivity low.
Many firms stay outside the formal system to avoid tax and regulation.
Tiny firms cannot reach economies of scale.
Most employment is informal and low-paid.
pts.ex: Link: 'the challenge is wages, not jobs' (IE, 2 Nov).

pts.t: Few firms are large enough to supply global value chains.
A few large groups dominate while the base stays weak.

answer.h: Measures to help them scale up

pts.t: Let firms keep benefits for a period after crossing thresholds.
pts.ex: Revised MSME definition.

pts.t: Lend on digital transaction records, not just collateral.
pts.ex: TReDS for invoice discounting; CGTMSE credit guarantees.

pts.t: Penalise late payments to MSMEs.
Self-certification, fewer inspections, decriminalised minor offences.
pts.ex: FM: policy built on trusting business.

pts.t: Common facilities, testing labs and tool rooms for MSME clusters.

pts.k: Link to big firms and PLI
pts.t: Bring MSMEs into supply chains of large manufacturers and incentive schemes.
pts.ex: PLI rewards additional production.

pts.t: Apprenticeships and easy registration bring firms into the formal economy.
pts.ex: Udyam registration.

answer.t: India will become a manufacturing power only when its micro firms are free and able to grow; trust, credit and a growth-friendly policy can fill the missing middle.

title: PM: India to add 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity in the next 10-11 years
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Climate change; Investment models · GS2 › International agreements (Paris Agreement)
summary: At the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, the PM set a goal of adding 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in 10–11 years, noting India met its Paris target of half its capacity from non-fossil sources five years early.
evolution: Editorial: E100 alone will not secure energy; diesel dominates oil demand.
Editorial page: energy security depends on electrification and how we do it.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity addition goal for the next decade.
ideas: Early delivery on Paris: India pledged that half its installed power capacity would be non-fossil and met it in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
GS2 · Paris Agreement / GS3 · Climate
Meeting the Paris non-fossil capacity target five years early strengthens India's credibility in climate negotiations.
A bigger next step: the PM announced 500 GW of new non-fossil capacity over the next 10–11 years, calling the target difficult but achievable.
GS3 · Energy transition
India's new 500 GW goal signals that the energy transition is moving from targets met to scale-up.
Clean energy as energy security: the PM said clean-energy investment helped India avert a worse energy crisis during the West Asia war.
GS3 · Energy security / GS2 · Foreign policy
Domestic clean power insulates India from fossil-fuel shocks abroad.
Investment drives the shift: the PM cited large flows into renewables over the past decade and big opportunities ahead.
GS3 · Investment
Sustained private investment is what turns renewable targets into installed capacity.
Capacity is not yet generation: a majority of installed capacity is non-fossil, but intermittent sources need storage, grids and flexible supply to deliver reliable power.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Installed capacity must be matched by storage and transmission to become reliable clean electricity.
keywords: Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC)
A country's climate pledge under the Paris Agreement
GS2 · International agreements
India's early achievement of its NDC capacity target shows climate action matching commitment.
Installed capacity vs generation
Plant size versus electricity actually produced
GS3 · Energy
Non-fossil sources lead in installed capacity but still trail in generation share.
Energy storage
Batteries and pumped hydro that store power for later
GS3 · Energy
Storage is the missing link that makes solar and wind reliable.
Energy sovereignty
Meeting energy needs from domestic sources
GS3 · Energy security
Renewables move India from import dependence towards energy sovereignty.
data: Installed non-fossil capacity, and its share of total installed capacity of 558.89 GW
Central Electricity Authority, via IE
GS3 · Energy
India has 308 GW of non-fossil capacity, 55.1% of total installed capacity (CEA).
Year India met its Paris pledge of 50% installed capacity from non-fossil sources, five years early
PM, at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, via IE
GS2 · Paris Agreement
India met its 50% non-fossil capacity pledge in 2025, five years ahead of the 2030 target.
examples: Paris target met five years early
50% non-fossil installed capacity reached in 2025
GS2 · International agreements · GS3 · Climate · Essay
India meeting its Paris capacity target early shows a developing country leading by delivery, not just pledges.
Clean energy and the West Asia war
Renewables cushioned India from a worse energy crisis
GS1 · Globalisation · GS2 · Energy security · GS3 · Energy
The West Asia war showed that every solar panel at home is a hedge against shocks abroad.
pyqs: Meeting 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030 and shifting subsidies.
Challenges for India's energy security and measures.
Energy independence through clean technology by 2047.
India's changing climate policy in international fora.
Status and targets of renewable energy.

trend.t: Renewable questions moved from status and targets (2016) and solar costs (2015, 2020) to whether India will meet 50% renewables by 2030 (2022) and energy independence through clean technology by 2047 (2025). In 2026 the frame became energy security with growth and sustainability.
trend.watch: Renewable targets and energy security now come almost every year. Prepare the Paris target met early, the next goals, and the challenges of storage and grids.

potential: "India's energy transition has moved from setting targets to building systems." Examine with reference to renewable energy. (15 marks)
What challenges must India overcome to add 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in the next decade? (10 marks)

practice.q: What challenges must India overcome to add 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in the next decade?

answer.t: India has 308 GW of non-fossil capacity, 55.1% of the total (CEA), and met its Paris capacity target in 2025; the PM now seeks 500 GW more in 10–11 years.

pts.t: Solar and wind need batteries and pumped hydro for evening and night demand.
Grids must carry power from resource-rich to demand centres.
Large projects face land acquisition and local resistance.
Cost of capital and discom finances.
Dependence on imported equipment.
Balancing variable supply with demand.
Mandates and incentives for batteries and pumped hydro.
Expand inter-state transmission.
Improve finances to sustain purchases.
Cut dependence on imports.

answer.t: Having met its Paris target early, India's next test is turning capacity into reliable, round-the-clock clean power.

title: Steel policy for 2047 needs to shift focus — from protection to competition
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Montek S Ahluwalia, Shishir Gupta & Rishita Sachdeva, CSEP)
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effect on growth; Effects of liberalisation; Mineral resources · GS1 › Distribution of industries and mineral resources; Effects of globalisation · GS2 › Government policies
summary: On the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047, the writers argue Indian steel is profitable because it is protected, not efficient, and that duties, quality-control orders and the iron-ore export duty must be phased down.
ideas: Big but not yet competitive: India has risen to the world's second-largest steel producer, but the draft policy's goal of global competitiveness needs a clear meaning, as high profits come from protection, not efficiency.
GS3 · Industrial policy
High profitability under protection is not the same as global competitiveness.
Cheap ore, underpaid states: a 30% export duty on high-grade iron ore keeps domestic ore far below global prices, subsidising steelmakers at the cost of mineral-rich regions and exploration.
GS3 · Mineral policy / GS1 · Resource regions
Export duties on ore transfer value from mineral-rich regions to steelmakers and discourage mining.
